assertion: Students who completed a Colorado college program in 2017-18 earned about 55% more than state residents with only a high school diploma, according to a new study. That gap, called a wage premium, was the second lowest in the country.
measure: earnings of college graduates vs high school graduates by state, College Scorecard program earnings
independent_value: IHE: Colorado 55%, ranked 49 of 50 (second lowest); Alaska last at 28%. Deseret: Colorado 55%. The HEA cohort also includes 2018-19 completers, a minor omission.

assertion: Colorado degree or certificate holders earned about $61,000 a year on average in the four years after graduating ... High school diploma holders earned about $39,000 a year in the four years after graduating. While that's a difference of more than $20,000, it still falls short of the national average of closer to $26,000 and a 76% wage premium.
inaccuracy: The claim says Colorado holders earned $61,000 'on average in the four years after graduating'; the evidence says $60,800 is a median measured in the fourth year after completion (calendar 2022-23), not an average over four years.
independent_value: IHE: median $60,800 vs $39,200; national premium 76%; HEA FAQ: median earnings four years later. $34,808 x 1.76 gives about $26,450 national gap.

assertion: High school graduates on average earn $39,174 a year. That's compared to a national average of $34,808 a year.
inaccuracy: The claim says high school graduates 'on average' earn $39,174 against a 'national average of $34,808'; the HEA FAQ says $34,808 is a median for working 25-34-year-olds with no college, and that the national benchmark was recalculated to $35,678 in October 2026.
independent_value: HEA FAQ: national $34,808 (median, ages 25-34). IHE: Colorado HS $39,200.

assertion: In Colorado, 11% of students completed a college program in 2017-18 that resulted in earnings below what a high school graduate made, the data shows.
measure: Colorado share of college program completers earning below high school graduates
reason: No readable source states 11%. 'Resulted in' is wording for an association, not a causal assertion. HEA's FAQ itself says the data cannot show the program caused the earnings.
why_no_page: HEA state snapshot and interactive load as JavaScript shells with no Colorado text; IHE and Deseret do not give the 11%.
searched: HEA Group Payoff of College Credentials Colorado second lowest

assertion: That's almost double the national average. About a third of those students earned cosmetology certificates.
measure: Colorado share of college program completers earning below high school graduates
reason: No readable source states the national share or the cosmetology third. IHE confirms cosmetology credentials earn less than high school graduates in every state but Minnesota.
why_no_page: HEA interactive is JavaScript-rendered; IHE and Deseret do not give these figures.
searched: HEA Group Colorado cosmetology certificates below high school earnings

assertion: Colorado bachelor's degree holders make $68,264, earnings near the national average of $67,988. Associate degree holders make $51,848, lower than the $53,315 national average. Certificate holders earn about $45,214, which is higher than the national average of $42,509.
measure: Colorado bachelor's associate certificate median earnings four years after completion by state
reason: Level-specific figures sit in the HEA interactive, which did not render; not in the FAQ, IHE or Deseret text. Internally consistent with the roughly $61,000 overall figure.
why_no_page: HEA interactive is JavaScript-rendered; FAQ has no state tables.

assertion: If a program fails to show that it improves a student's pay higher than a high school diploma in two out of three consecutive years, it will lose eligibility to participate in federal direct student loan programs. The federal government will start to designate ineligible programs in the 2028-29 year.
independent_value: NPR: programs fail after two of three consecutive years; quotes the ed.gov fact sheet that programs 'could be designated as low-earning outcome programs beginning in the 2028-2029 award year'. Deseret quotes the DOE release on losing Direct Loan eligibility.

assertion: Colorado's high school diploma holders have higher pay than the national average.
warehouse_value: ACS 2023 median HS earnings 25+: Colorado $43,437 (Alaska $42,584, Utah $41,486, Wyoming $41,135); HEA $39,174 vs $34,808 national.
sql: SELECT state, geo_name, median_earnings_hs_graduate FROM census.acs_earnings_by_education WHERE "year"=2023 AND state IN ('08','49','02','56')
independent_value: IHE: Colorado high school completers $39,200, 'significantly more' than most states.

assertion: The department has not restricted any college programs on the basis of low earnings, the spokesperson said.
speaker: Colorado Department of Higher Education spokesperson
measure: state higher education agency restricted programs low earnings Colorado
reason: Agency statement about its own conduct; no independent record found. The federal rule is not yet in force.
why_no_page: cdhe.colorado.gov returned HTTP 403; the Chalkbeat Oct 19 Workforce Pell story shows the state rejecting some Workforce Pell programs for completion and job-rate standards, a different program.

assertion: Colorado Mountain College has created a process to eliminate programs that don't benefit students ... such as one used to cut a portion of its outdoor education program.
speaker: Matt Gianneschi
measure: Colorado Mountain College program discontinuation outdoor education
inaccuracy: The claim says the process removes programs that do not benefit students; CMC's Nov 17, 2026 release says the cut followed a review of student demand, industry and community needs.
independent_value: CMC discontinues the Associate of Arts in outdoor education and certificates in avalanche science, rope rescue and fly-fishing guide, after a comprehensive review.
